docs.text: Crosswork CNC Hands-on ¶ This is the operator lab for Cisco Crosswork Network Controller (CNC) 7.1. You will use one shared controller and a Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) topology. Menu names follow the CNC 7.1 UI. The room has one controller. A change you commit is visible to every seat. Use the seat number on the whiteboard in every name, color, and VPN id. Storyline ¶ You take the controller from a quiet maintenance state to a network you can see, explain, and change in a controlled way: Bring the controller and the CML lab up. Confirm the platform, the providers, and data collection. Read the topology. Read inventory, configuration, alarms, events, and performance. Compare a router-owned SR policy with a controller-owned SR policy. Provision one L3VPN and steer it onto that policy. Walk through Local Congestion Mitigation (LCM). The instructor owns any live commit. Tour Zero Touch Provisioning (ZTP) on screen. Ask the lab assistant one inventory question through the MCP server, then decide the next check yourself. Lab values ¶ Copy this table into your notes and fill it from the whiteboard. Keep passwords out of the guide, out of chat, and out of screenshots you share. Item Your value Seat number CNC UI URL CML URL and lab name Assistant URL Headend hostname Endpoint hostname PCE-initiated policy name pta-pce-seat-<seat> PCE-initiated color 200 + seat L3VPN service name PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> Route distinguisher and route target assigned by the instructor LCM tactical color reserved by the instructor Colors 200 through 220 are for student PCE-initiated policies. The LCM tactical color is reserved so a mitigation policy cannot collide with your lab policy. Suggested schedule ¶ Two lab sessions, after the morning architecture briefing. Session Chapters Intent A 1 to 4 The network is visible and the devices are understandable B 5 and 6 One SR policy and one L3VPN, with steering you can point at on the map C 7 to 9 Congestion workflow, ZTP tour, assistant question Chapters 1 and 7 start with an instructor action. Wait for that action before you click. How to read each chapter ¶ Each chapter has an objective, the clicks, the result you should see, and a short "done when" list. Router work in this lab is show output. Configuration changes go through CNC, and only in the chapters that say so. View this guide ¶ From this folder, with the existing virtual environment: source venv/bin/activate mkdocs serve Open the local URL MkDocs prints. mkdocs build writes the static site under site/ . What changed from the first outline ¶ The nine chapters you listed are the lab. A few placements changed so the day matches CNC 7.1 and a shared CML lab. CNC management includes providers and the Data Gateway. SR-PCE, NSO, and collection are the reason later chapters succeed. They belong with platform health, before the topology work. Device configuration templates stay in the element-management chapter. In CNC 7.1 they live under Device Management. The NSO L2VPN and L3VPN function-pack templates are a different library. You meet those in the L3VPN chapter, when a provision action uses them. SR-TE is observe-then-create. A PCC-initiated policy is already on a headend. You learn it from CNC. A PCE-initiated policy is the one you create, with your own color. LCM stays in the outline, in Manual mode. CNC 7.1 can recommend tactical SR-TE policies when SNMP utilization crosses a threshold. A CML lab often shows 0% utilization, so a missing recommendation is a valid outcome. One instructor commits a recommendation if the data supports it. Students leave Automated mode untouched. Bandwidth on Demand is the fallback live demonstration when you want a PCE action and the links are idle. ZTP stays a screen tour. The same rule covers image upload, serial-number enrollment, and template deployment. The MCP chapter matches the assistant you have. The live question is the inventory count the server can answer. Remediation stays an operator decision. Session and write tools stay unused. A checkpoint page collects the few failures that stop the room: maintenance still on, CML nodes down, provider unreachable, collection idle, NSO out of sync. An L2VPN service is the same provisioning pattern as the L3VPN. This lab provisions one L3VPN so every seat finishes.

docs.text: 1. Preparation ¶ Time: 30 minutes, most of it waiting. Objective: Leave maintenance mode, start the CML lab, and log in to a controller that is ready for work. Instructor One person moves the maintenance slider, and one person starts the CML lab. Ask everyone else to stay logged out until you say the UI is back. Maintenance mode shuts the applications down gracefully, and bringing them back takes several minutes. During that window the UI is the wrong place to click. 1.1 Leave maintenance mode ¶ Maintenance mode is how CNC stops itself cleanly for a reboot, a backup, or a restore. After a reboot that began in maintenance mode, the cluster comes back in maintenance mode and waits for the slider to be turned off. The instructor does this while the room watches the screen: Sign in to the CNC UI at the URL on the whiteboard. If the browser reports a certificate warning, check that the hostname matches the whiteboard URL, then use the exception the instructor demonstrates. That exception is for this lab URL. Go to Administration > Settings > System Settings > Maintenance Mode . If a popup already offers to turn maintenance mode off, accept it. If the Maintenance slider is On, drag it to Off and confirm. If the cluster was rebooted in maintenance mode and you see no popup, turn the slider On, wait until the mode is fully on, then turn it Off again. CNC 7.1 uses that extra toggle to let the applications start cleanly. Wait. The applications need several minutes. Leave the session alone while they restart. Result: The maintenance slider stays Off, the UI loads the normal home page, and other users can sign in. Students sign in only after the instructor confirms that step. 1.2 Start the CML lab ¶ The routers, the SR-PCE, and the traffic in this class come from the CML topology named on the whiteboard. Open the CML URL from the whiteboard. Open the PTA lab. If the lab is already started, leave it running. If the lab is stopped, start it once. A second start from another seat fights the first one. Wait until every node the instructor listed shows as booted. Open one provider-edge console only if the instructor asks. Confirm the management interface is up. Save configuration commands for later chapters, and only the ones CNC sends. Result: The lab is booted. CNC can reach the devices after the providers and the Data Gateway are healthy. You confirm that reachability in the next chapter. 1.3 Sign in and look around ¶ Sign in to CNC with the account the instructor gives you. Land on the home page. You should see the application launcher and a topology entry point. Open the account menu only far enough to see which user you are. Sign out at the end of the day. Leave the user list unchanged. Result: You are in the UI as yourself, and the controller is in normal operating mode. Done when ¶ Maintenance mode is Off. The CML lab is booted. You are signed in. You have your seat number and the lab-values table from the home page.

docs.text: 2. CNC management ¶ Time: 40 minutes. Objective: Decide whether the platform is healthy enough for topology, inventory, traffic engineering, and service provisioning. You are reading the system, not rebuilding it. The three dependencies for the rest of the lab: Later work Depends on Topology and SR policies SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS and PCEP from the routers Inventory, alarms, interface utilization Crosswork Data Gateway collection L3VPN provisioning NSO provider, devices in sync 2.1 Application health ¶ Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager . Open the cluster or application view the page offers. Find these applications and read the state next to each one: Platform infrastructure Optimization Engine Active Topology Element Management Functions / Device Lifecycle Management Data Gateway related services A state of Running or Healthy is what you want before chapter 3. Degraded and Down belong on the checkpoint page. Result: You can name the applications this lab uses and their states. Leave restart, node drain, and maintenance controls untouched. You already finished maintenance mode in chapter 1. 2.2 Providers ¶ CNC learns the routed topology from SR-PCE. CNC provisions services through NSO. Both are providers. Go to Administration > Manage Provider Access . Find the SR-PCE provider. Read its reachability and the protocol state. You want the provider reachable, with the topology feed up. Find the NSO provider. Read its reachability. You want NSO reachable. Open the provider detail far enough to see the credential profile name. The profile is a pointer. The password stays in the profile store. Result: SR-PCE and NSO are both reachable. If either is down, stop and use the checkpoint page before chapter 5 or chapter 6. Chapters 3 and 4 can still teach the screens. 2.3 Data Gateway ¶ Interface counters, inventory detail, syslog, and SNMP traps arrive through a Crosswork Data Gateway (CDG). LCM in chapter 7 reads interface utilization from this collection, through SNMP. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management , or the Data Gateway page linked from Crosswork Manager. Confirm the gateway is enrolled and the pool is up. Open one attached device and confirm a data gateway is mapped to it. A device with no gateway mapping has no inventory refresh and no interface counters. If a collection job or destination is listed, read its status. Healthy collection is the bar. Result: You can point at the gateway that will feed alarms, inventory, and utilization. 2.4 What you leave alone ¶ Credential profiles, AAA, certificates, backup jobs, and licensing are visible from Administration and from Device Management > Credential Profiles . Open a profile only if a device is unreachable and the instructor asks you to compare the profile name. Editing a profile on a shared controller locks every other seat out of that device. Backup and restore put the cluster into maintenance mode. They are out of scope for this session. Done when ¶ Optimization Engine, Active Topology, and element management are Running or Healthy. The SR-PCE provider is reachable. The NSO provider is reachable. A Data Gateway is enrolled and mapped to the lab devices.

docs.text: 3. Active Topology (CAT) ¶ Time: 45 minutes. Objective: Use Crosswork Active Topology to answer where a device sits, how it is connected, and which layer you are looking at. Active Topology is the map. Optimization Engine supplies the traffic-engineering view on top of the same topology. You will switch between those views so the two products stay distinct in your notes. 3.1 Open the map ¶ From the main menu, open Topology . Wait for the devices from the CML lab to appear. A topology that stays empty usually means the SR-PCE provider is up and BGP-LS is down, or the CML nodes are still booting. Check chapter 2 and the checkpoint page. Switch between the logical map and the geographical map if both are offered. The logical map is the one you will use for the rest of the day. Zoom to the two provider edges named on your lab-values sheet. Those are the headend and the endpoint for chapters 5 and 6. Result: You can find both PEs and at least one path between them. 3.2 Read a device and a link ¶ Select the headend. Open the details panel. Record the hostname, the management address, and the reachability state. Select a core link that sits on a path between the headend and the endpoint. In the link details, record: IGP metric TE metric, if one is shown Interface names on each side Utilization, if a value is shown Adjacency SID or SRv6 adjacency information, if the link shows it Say out loud which value a PCE would minimize if the objective was IGP metric, and which value it would minimize if the objective was TE metric. Utilization on a CML link is often 0%. Write down the number you actually see. Chapter 7 uses it. Result: One device record and one link record in your notes. 3.3 Layers and filters ¶ The map can show more than one underlay. PTA's core work is segment routing, with SRv6 as the policy type when the whiteboard says so. Open the layer or protocol selector. Turn on the IGP layer and confirm the links you care about are still there. Turn on the SR-MPLS or SRv6 layer that matches the whiteboard. Adjacency and prefix SID information belongs to this layer. If a Flex-Algo layer is present, note the algorithm id and leave it. Flex-Algo is a map fact in this lab, not a configuration task. Apply a filter or device group that shows only the lab core, if a group already exists. Creating a new group is optional and is an instructor choice on a shared map. Result: You can turn the TE layer on and still recognize the same two PEs. 3.4 Dashboard tiles ¶ Return to the home page or the topology dashboard. Read the tiles that summarize device reachability, link state, and policy count. If a tile shows zero SR policies, that is acceptable before chapter 5. Write the number down so you can compare it after you create a PCE-initiated policy. Result: You have a baseline count of policies and of reachable devices. Done when ¶ Both lab PEs are on the map and reachable. You recorded metric and utilization for one core link. You can show the IGP layer and the segment-routing layer. You know the baseline SR policy count.

docs.text: 4. Element management (EMF) ¶ Time: 60 minutes. Objective: Use the CNC 7.1 element-management functions to read inventory, archived configuration, a configuration template, alarms, events, and performance. Deploy nothing from this chapter. Element Management Functions in CNC 7.1 cover device onboarding, inventory, faults, metrics, software images, configuration backup, and configuration templates. ZTP is part of the same lifecycle guide. You will tour ZTP in chapter 8 so this hour stays on "what is on the device today." 4.1 Network devices and inventory ¶ Go to Device Management > Network Devices . Find the headend. Read operational state, reachability, and the credential profile name. Confirm a Data Gateway is associated with the device. Chapter 2 introduced that mapping. This is where a missing mapping shows up as a device you cannot refresh. Go to Device Management > Network Inventory . Filter to the headend hostname or product family. Open the chassis, one route processor or line card, and one pluggable if the inventory has them. Open the alarm summary on that inventory row. You will come back to the full alarm list in section 4.4. Result: You can walk from a hostname to a chassis and a module, and you know whether the device is reachable. A device that stays unreachable for the whole session needs the checkpoint page: credentials, routing to the management address, and CML node state. Give it a few minutes after the lab boots before you call it failed. 4.2 Configuration backup ¶ CNC can archive device configuration, compare two archives, and restore. This lab uses the archive as a reader. Go to Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore . Find the headend. Open the latest archived configuration and identify the hostname and the segment-routing or BGP section the instructor points out. If two archives exist, open the compare view and name one difference, or state that the two archives match. Leave Schedule backup and Restore unused. Result: You have seen a real archived configuration for the headend and you know where a later change would show up. Automatic backup on configuration change, when it is enabled under Device Management > Configuration Preferences , is what makes this archive useful after chapter 6. Read the preference. Leave the values as you found them. 4.3 Configuration templates ¶ Device templates under Device Management are parameterized CLI (Apache Velocity template language). They are for repeating underlay or day-1 configuration across similar devices. They are a different store from the NSO L2VPN and L3VPN function-pack templates that chapter 6 uses. Go to Device Management > Configuration Templates . Open one existing template. Read the device types it targets and one variable it expects. Open Jobs only if a previous job is listed, and read its status. Close the template. Leave Create Template and every deploy action unused. Result: You can explain the difference between this template library and the service template NSO applies when you provision an L3VPN. Deploying a template from this screen writes CLI to live routers. That write is out of scope for a shared class. 4.4 Alarms and events ¶ Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events . Stay on Alarms . Use the category list to see system, network, and device alarms as separate sets. Filter to the headend if the filter allows it. If an alarm is present, record severity, source, and whether it is acknowledged. Leave acknowledge, clear, and annotate unused unless the instructor gives you a lab alarm of your own. Switch Show from Alarms to Events . Read the newest event. An event is a moment in time. An alarm remains until it clears. Use one sentence to put the event you found into one of those two buckets. Result: You can open both views and you did not clear someone else's alarm. An empty alarm list is a valid result on a healthy CML lab. Write "no active device alarms" and move on. 4.5 Performance ¶ Link colors on the topology map come from interface utilization collected for Optimization Engine. Element management adds polling policies and device-level metrics. Go to Device Management > Performance Policies , or the performance page under Device Management on your build. Open one existing policy. Read which devices or groups it covers, how often it polls, and which threshold raises an alarm. Return to the headend in Network Inventory or Network Devices and open the metrics or interface view. Compare one interface counter with the utilization you wrote down in chapter 3. Leave the policy inactive/active switch as you found it. A new polling policy on every seat multiplies SNMP load on the lab. Result: You can say where a threshold is defined, and you can point at one live counter. Done when ¶ The headend is in Network Devices and in Network Inventory. You opened an archived configuration and a device template, and you deployed neither. You opened Alarms and Events. You can point at the polling policy that would raise a threshold alarm.

docs.text: Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events . Stay on Alarms . Use the category list to see system, network, and device alarms as separate sets. Filter to the headend if the filter allows it. docs.text: 5. Segment Routing and Traffic Engineering ¶ Time: 75 minutes. Objective: Explain a PCC-initiated policy that the headend already owns, then create one PCE-initiated SR policy from CNC with your own name and color. Use the policy type on the whiteboard. For this PTA lab that type is SRv6 when the core is SRv6, and SR-MPLS when the core is SR-MPLS. The CNC pages are the same shape. Pick the tab that matches the whiteboard and stay on it. 5.1 Words you need ¶ Term Meaning in this lab PCC The headend router. It may ask SR-PCE for a path, and it can own a policy that was configured on the router. PCE SR-PCE. It computes paths and can instantiate a policy on a headend through PCEP. PCC-initiated The policy configuration lives on the headend. CNC learns the policy from SR-PCE and draws it. PCE-initiated You create the policy in CNC. SR-PCE pushes it to the headend. The headend shows it as delegated to the PCE. Color A number that identifies the intent. Steering in chapter 6 binds a VPN to a color. Candidate path One way to reach the endpoint. Preference chooses among candidate paths. 5.2 Find the PCC-initiated policy ¶ The instructor prepares one PCC-initiated policy before class, on the headend, with a color outside the 200 + seat range. You do not type that router configuration. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering . Open the SRv6 or SR-MPLS tab named on the whiteboard. Filter or sort the policy table until you find the PCC-initiated policy. The initiation column says PCC. Record headend, endpoint, color, preference, and the active candidate path. Select the policy and show it on the map. Name two hops on the drawn path. If the table has no PCC row, say so. The rest of this chapter still works. The live create is the PCE-initiated policy. Tell the instructor the prepared PCC policy is missing. Result: You can point at a policy the router owns, or you have recorded that the prepared policy is absent. On the headend console, if the instructor opens one, these commands support the same story. Read them. Leave configuration mode. show segment-routing traffic-eng policy show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv4 peer On an IPv6-only SRv6 headend the peer command may be the IPv6 form: show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv6 peer Use the form the instructor shows. In the output, find the color of the PCC policy and the PCE peer address. 5.3 Create a PCE-initiated policy ¶ Your policy name is pta-pce-seat-<seat> . Your color is 200 + seat . Two seats that reuse a color will fight over steering in chapter 6. Stay on Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering , on the same SRv6 or SR-MPLS tab. Start the create action and choose PCE-initiated . Set: Name: pta-pce-seat-<seat> Headend: the headend from your lab-values sheet Endpoint: the endpoint from your lab-values sheet Color: 200 + seat Optimization objective: IGP metric, unless the instructor writes a different objective Leave bandwidth, affinity, and disjoint constraints empty unless the instructor adds one constraint for the whole room. Preview the path. You want a path that passes through the core, from your headend to your endpoint. If the preview is empty, stop. An empty preview means SR-PCE has no topology or no SID reachability. Use the checkpoint page. Committing an empty path teaches the wrong lesson. When the preview shows a path, provision the policy. Return to the policy table. Your row shows initiation PCE , your color, and an operational state that is up. Select the row and display the path on the map. Result: A PCE-initiated policy exists for your seat, and the map draws it. 5.4 Confirm on the headend ¶ Ask the instructor for a console on the headend, or watch the instructor's console. show segment-routing traffic-eng policy Find pta-pce-seat-<seat> . In the same output, the PCC-initiated policy is still present. The difference is ownership: one policy is configured on the router, and the other was instantiated by the PCE. If your policy is missing on the router and present in CNC as down, the usual causes are a PCEP session that is down, a color conflict, or a headend that cannot place the SIDs. Stay with the checkpoint page. Delete only your own down policy, and only when the instructor agrees. 5.5 Clean-up rule ¶ Keep this policy until chapter 6 has steered a VPN onto its color. At the end of the day, delete only pta-pce-seat-<seat> . Leave the PCC-initiated policy in place for the next session. Done when ¶ You can say who owns the PCC-initiated policy and who owns yours. Your PCE-initiated policy is up, with your color, and it is drawn on the map. You saw both policies in show segment-routing traffic-eng policy , or you have a written reason the headend console was unavailable.

docs.text: 6. Intent-based L3VPN provisioning ¶ Time: 75 minutes. Objective: Create one L3VPN from CNC. NSO renders the device configuration from the service model and the function-pack template. Steer the VPN onto the PCE-initiated policy from chapter 5. The UI path is Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO) . CNC 7.1 provisions IETF L3VPN network models through NSO. You fill in the service intent. You do not paste CLI, and you do not edit the XML template on the NSO server. 6.1 What you are about to commit ¶ Each seat creates a different service: Field Value Service name PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> Endpoints the two PEs on your lab-values sheet, using the attachment points the instructor assigns Route distinguisher and route targets the pair on the whiteboard for your seat Steering preferred path, bound to color 200 + seat Transport the same SRv6 or SR-MPLS type you used in chapter 5 Preferred path is the steering method for this lab because the map can show the VPN sitting on the policy you just created. On-demand next hop (ODN) is the other method: the headend builds a path when it receives a route with that color. Read the ODN choice in the form so you recognize it, then select preferred path. If the PTA service profile on this controller exposes only one steering knob, use the one the instructor names. Record which one you used. 6.2 Create the service ¶ Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO) . Open the L3VPN service type. Create a service named PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> . Select the instance profile or VPN profile the instructor named. That profile points at the NSO L3VPN template. You are choosing it, not editing it. Enter the route distinguisher and route targets for your seat. Add the two endpoints. For each endpoint set the device, the attachment circuit or interface, and the PE-CE routing the instructor specified. A lab that uses a static route on one side and BGP on the other is still one L3VPN. Follow the whiteboard. Set the underlay transport to the policy type from chapter 5. Set steering to preferred path and select color 200 + seat , or select the policy pta-pce-seat-<seat> if the form asks for a policy name. Run Dry run before Commit . Read the preview far enough to see your service name, your two endpoints, and the color. A preview that names another seat's VPN is the wrong form. Close it and start again from your own service name. Commit. Open the service and read the sync state. In sync means NSO and the devices agree. Out of sync belongs on the checkpoint page before you troubleshoot the VPN itself. Result: PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> is committed and in sync. 6.3 See it on the map ¶ Open Services & Traffic Engineering > VPN Services , or the service overlay the provisioning page links to. Select your VPN. Show the service path and the underlay policy together. Confirm the underlay is pta-pce-seat-<seat> , or a path whose color is 200 + seat . Result: You can show a neighbour the service and the SR policy it rides. 6.4 Read the effect on the PE ¶ On the headend, with the instructor's console: show bgp vpnv4 unicast summary show bgp vpnv6 unicast summary Use the address family this lab actually runs. PTA's IPv6 core still may carry an IPv4 VPN, an IPv6 VPN, or both. The whiteboard says which summary command should show your VRF. Then: show vrf show segment-routing traffic-eng policy You want the VRF for PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> and the same PCE-initiated policy as chapter 5. Leave configuration mode. 6.5 Templates, stated once ¶ The XML templates in the NSO L3VPN function pack are what turned your form into CLI. Device Management templates from chapter 4 did not. If a dry run fails with a template or profile error, the profile name is the thing to check. Editing the package on the NSO server is an instructor action outside this class. 6.6 Clean-up rule ¶ Keep your VPN until you have shown it on the map. At the end of the day, delete PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> from the provisioning page, then delete your PCE-initiated policy. Deleting the policy first, while the VPN still prefers it, leaves the service with nowhere to steer. Order is VPN, then policy. Done when ¶ Dry run showed your service name, your endpoints, and your color. The service is in sync. The VPN overlay draws your service on your PCE-initiated policy. You can say which template store rendered the CLI.

docs.text: 7. Closed-loop congestion mitigation ¶ Time: 45 minutes. Objective: Read Local Congestion Mitigation (LCM) on CNC 7.1, explain the closed loop, and leave the shared network in Manual mode. 7.1 Lab decision ¶ LCM is a real Optimization Engine feature in CNC 7.1, and it is the right exercise for this chapter. It looks for congestion on a timer, estimates traffic that can be moved off a hot interface, and recommends tactical traffic-engineering (TTE) SR policies around that interface. In Manual mode an operator previews the recommendation and then commits it. SR-PCE deploys the tactical policies. When the interface cools, LCM recommends removal. LCM sees congestion through SNMP interface counters collected by the Data Gateway. It also needs a discovered IGP domain (the BGP-LS link-state instance-id ), an alternate local path, and a tactical color that no other policy uses. A CML topology often reports 0% utilization , because the links carry no traffic. LCM then has nothing to mitigate. That outcome still completes this chapter. Record the utilization and the threshold, and explain why the operational dashboard has no recommendation. Instructor Keep the domain in Manual mode. Automated mode deploys tactical policies without a human commit, and in later releases it also requires a fully gRPC-compliant domain. Students do not change the mode. Commit a recommendation only when one domain shows a real recommendation and you want the room to see a single deploy. Use the reserved tactical color. Students do not click Commit all . If you want a live PCE action and every interface is idle, use Bandwidth on Demand as a demonstration. BWoD asks for a path with a bandwidth number. It does not need a hot link. It is a different feature. Show it from the instructor console, and keep the student exercise on the LCM screens. 7.2 Open the domain ¶ Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Local Congestion Mitigation . Read the domain card. The domain id comes from the IGP link-state instance-id advertised in BGP-LS. Record: LCM status (enabled or not) Operation mode Urgency The description, which defaults to "LCM Startup Config" on a fresh configuration If the card says the domain is not configured, stop and let the instructor open Configure . The room uses one LCM configuration. Result: You know the domain id and the operation mode. The mode you want to see is Manual. 7.3 Read the thresholds and the loop ¶ Open Interface Thresholds . Find one core interface you recorded in chapter 3. Read its utilization threshold. Compare that threshold with the utilization you wrote down from the topology map. Say which side of the threshold the interface is on. Open Configuration . Read the congestion check interval, the optimization objective, and the operation mode. Leave every field as you found it. Walk the loop in your own words: CDG polls interface counters with SNMP. LCM compares utilization with the interface threshold on the check interval. A hot interface produces a TTE SR policy recommendation that stays local to that hop. In Manual mode the recommendation waits on the operational dashboard. Commit sends the tactical policy through SR-PCE. A later check recommends deletion when the interface is under the threshold again. Result: You can teach the loop from the screens, with your own utilization number in the story. 7.4 Recommendations ¶ Open the Operational Dashboard for the domain. Use the "Recommendations available" link when the card shows it. If a recommendation is listed, read urgency and the interfaces it would bypass. Preview it on the map. Then stop. The instructor commits, or nobody commits. If the dashboard is empty, write the sentence: "No recommendation, utilization is below the threshold." Include the two numbers. Open Operational History if it has rows from an earlier demo, and read one commit or one removal. History is part of the product even when this hour adds no new row. Result: You have either previewed one recommendation or recorded why none exists. 7.5 What you leave alone ¶ The operation-mode control stays on Manual. Commit all stays with the instructor. The tactical color stays the reserved color, and it stays off your chapter 5 policy. Per-interface threshold edits are an instructor tool for a demo. A room full of lowered thresholds creates a pile of recommendations against empty CML links. Done when ¶ You can open the LCM domain, the thresholds, and the configuration. You compared one interface's utilization with its threshold. You can describe what a commit would deploy, and you did not deploy it yourself. You know BWoD is the instructor's fallback when the lab has no congestion to show.

docs.text: 8. Lifecycle management and ZTP ¶ Time: 20 minutes. Objective: Walk the Zero Touch Provisioning screens so you can recognize images, configuration files, serial numbers, profiles, and devices. Leave every router in its current boot state. CNC 7.1 puts ZTP under element management: Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning . Classic ZTP uses DHCP and HTTP so a new router can pull an image and a configuration. Secure ZTP (RFC 8572) adds ownership vouchers and a signed exchange. This controller may show both. The PTA lab routers are already onboarded through the normal device inventory. They are the wrong devices to reload into ZTP during class. 8.1 Tour ¶ Work down this list. Open each page, read the columns, and close it. Device Management > Software Management . This is the image and SMU store. Read one image name and the platform family, if any file is present. Upload nothing. Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning > Configuration files . These are ZTP day-0 scripts, with replaceable parameters. They are a third store, different from Device Management templates and from NSO service templates. Open one file if it exists and find a single placeholder. Download the sample XR script only if the instructor wants the room to see the comments. Upload nothing. Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning > Serial Numbers & Ownership . A device enters ZTP when its serial number is known here. Read the columns. Add no serial and import no CSV. docs.text: 9. Proactive assurance and the MCP server ¶ Time: 40 minutes. Objective: See where CNC monitors service and device health, then ask the lab assistant one question that it can answer from a live Crosswork tool. You decide what to do with the answer. 9.1 Assurance on the controller ¶ You already used device alarms, events, and performance policies in chapter 4. Two more CNC 7.1 applications sit above that, when they are installed on this cluster: Application What an operator uses it for Service Health A service-level view of the L2VPN and L3VPN you provisioned, with symptoms against the rules the operator enabled Health Insights KPI monitoring and alerts driven by logic the operator attached to devices From the main menu or the application list, open Service Health if it is installed. Find PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> if the service view has reached it. Read the health state and one symptom or rule name. If your service is absent, the collector has not scored it yet. Note the time and continue. Scoring can lag a new provision. Open Health Insights only if it is installed. Read one existing KPI profile. Enable no new KPI. A new profile on a shared cluster adds collection for every seat. If either application is missing from this single-VM lab, record "not installed" and continue with section 9.2. The MCP exercise is the required part of this chapter. Result: You know whether service health is scoring your VPN, and you left KPI enablement unchanged. 9.2 The assistant and MCP ¶ The lab assistant is a chat page. When you ask a question, the assistant may call tools on an MCP server. That server is what talks to Crosswork. The tools listed in the assistant sidebar are the only live data the assistant can fetch. Anything else in the reply is explanation, and you treat it as explanation until you confirm it in the CNC UI. The instructor starts the assistant and the MCP server before this chapter. You receive the assistant URL on the whiteboard. You do not receive, and you do not type, the controller password, an API token, or a client secret. Those stay in the instructor's configuration outside this guide. Open the assistant URL. Read the backend status in the sidebar. Continue when it is online. Read the tool list. Find the tool whose description is the inventory node count. That is the live tool for this lab. If the sidebar also lists session or ticket tools, leave them unused. This chapter does not delete sessions and does not change the controller. Result: The assistant is online and you can name the inventory tool. 9.3 One live question ¶ In the chat, ask: How many nodes are in the Crosswork inventory? Wait for the reply. Open the tool-call detail the UI shows for that turn. Check all of the following: The assistant called the inventory count tool. The reply contains a number. You can find a matching count under Device Management > Network Devices or Network Inventory . The two screens group equipment differently, so the numbers may differ by what each one counts. Write both numbers and one sentence on the difference you see. If they match, write that they match. If the tool call fails, the useful symptom is the error text, not a second guess from the model. A failure here usually means the assistant cannot authenticate to CNC or cannot reach the UI address. That is an instructor fix. Your earlier chapters already showed you the same inventory with your own login. Result: A number from the tool, compared with the number you read in Device Management. 9.4 Remediation stays with you ¶ Ask a second question that does not require a write tool: The inventory count is <the number you just verified>. The CML lab should have <the node count on the whiteboard> routers. What should an operator check first in Crosswork? A useful answer names checks you already know how to open: Reachability on Device Management > Network Devices The credential profile on that device Data Gateway mapping SR-PCE and NSO provider status Active alarms for that hostname Take one check the assistant named, open that CNC page, and confirm or contradict the suggestion with the screen. The screen wins. The assistant does not commit, delete, or provision. That is the remediation pattern for this lab: the assistant reads, the assistant suggests, the operator verifies, the operator changes the network only through the chapters that allow a commit. 9.5 What you leave out of the chat ¶ Passwords, tokens, ticket ids, and certificate contents A request to delete a session, a policy, a VPN, or a device Configuration text copied from another seat's dry run Done when ¶ You know whether Service Health and Health Insights are installed. The assistant answered the inventory question with a tool call. You compared that number with Device Management. You verified one suggested check on a CNC screen.
